doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Aaron Copland, and getting music in advance
summary: Raph worked once with Copland. He discusses how orchestral players now sometimes receive parts beforehand, whereas in the 50s and 60s they sight-read.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I worked with Aaron not much, with a little orchestra society. Bob Megel was playing first trumpet, I was playing first trombone. Aaron came into conduct his theater music and I think that’s the only time I ever worked for him, or with him. He conducted the concert, which means that we did two or three rehearsals and maybe one or two concerts. So I can’t really put a handle on it.
When you do a symphonic concert, do you get the music beforehand?
So it’s not that much different.

Well these days there’s more of a tendency for the orchestra, for the orchestral musicians to get the music beforehand. The Ridgefield Symphony sends out music. Other symphonies do, other bigger symphonies, and more better symphonies do the same. If it’s a matter of repertoire you’ve probably played or you probably know the excerpts. If it’s new stuff guys do ask for their parts but I never did and to my knowledge it wasn’t done a lot in the 50s and 60s. You just came in and played it, you came in and read it. I saw some astounding reading from classical musicians, really wonderful reading. I don’t know. Maybe the string players all had their part, I don’t know, but it was never apparent to me that they did. I was always under the impression that we were all in the same boat. It might have been naïve on my part.
Right. But I guess that’s part of the gig is to know the basic repertoire.
